author: Irenaeus of Lyons

text: The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets the dispensations of God

author: Irenaeus of Lyons

text: It is proper, then, that I should begin with the first and most important head, that is, God the Creator, who made the heaven and the earth, and all things that are therein

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: The fourfold Gospel — the Gospels can be neither more nor fewer than four (the classic patristic testimony to the four-Gospel canon, c. AD 180). Note the allusion 'the pillar and ground of the Church' quotes 1 Tim 3:15; confirm whether ANF sets it in quotation marks in the citations pass. text: It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are. For, since there are four zones of the world in which we live, and four principal winds, while the Church is scattered throughout all the world, and the pillar and ground of the Church is the Gospel and the spirit of life; it is fitting that she should have four pillars, breathing out immortality on every side, and vivifying men afresh.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: Context: Irenaeus is refuting the Gnostic claim that an impassible 'Christ' descended on the man Jesus and left him before the cross; he insists Jesus IS the Christ who suffered. The anointing described is the incarnate Son's anointing for his messianic mission (Isa 61:1; cf. Luke 4:18), NOT the beginning of the Son's divine sonship -- do not present it as adoptionist. The name 'Christ' is read in a trinitarian structure (Father anoints, Son is anointed, Spirit is the unction). Captured 2026-10-09 via fetch from New Advent (Roberts-Rambaut ANF); bounded excerpt from the end of III.18.3. The anointing belongs to the incarnate Son in his assumed humanity (cf. AH III.9.3, the Spirit descending on him at the Jordan); it implies neither that the Son is lesser in being than the Father nor that he became Son or Christ at the Jordan. Present the triad as Irenaeus's trinitarian reading of the name 'Christ', not as a ranking of the persons. Wording verified word-for-word against New Advent (Roberts & Rambaut, ANF vol. 1) by apologia-citations, 2026-10-09.
text: For in the name of Christ is implied, He that anoints, He that is anointed, and the unction itself with which He is anointed. And it is the Father who anoints, but the Son who is anointed by the Spirit, who is the unction, as the Word declares by Isaiah, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me, — pointing out both the anointing Father, the anointed Son, and the unction, which is the Spirit.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: Irenaeus's report (c. 180) of the Ebionites, listed among the heretical sects. Their 'opinions with respect to the Lord' are likened to Cerinthus (I.26.1: Jesus the son of Joseph and Mary by ordinary generation, with Christ descending on him after the baptism). Use ONLY as a hostile second-century REPORT of a sect the church rejected -- never as evidence for what the earliest Jerusalem church believed, and never quote its description of the Lord in the site's voice. Captured 2026-10-09 via fetch from New Advent (HGBJ-6, How God Became Jesus mining run). Wording verified word-for-word against New Advent by apologia-citations, 2026-10-09.
text: Those who are called Ebionites agree that the world was made by God; but their opinions with respect to the Lord are similar to those of Cerinthus and Carpocrates. They use the Gospel according to Matthew only, and repudiate the Apostle Paul, maintaining that he was an apostate from the law.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: Recapitulation — 'He who was the Son of God became the Son of man' so that man might receive the adoption and 'become the son of God.' The passage itself fences the meaning as ADOPTION ('receiving the adoption'), i.e. sonship by grace/participation, not becoming God by nature; frame it that way to avoid a compressed reader hearing ontological apotheosis. Captured via web fetch (New Advent, Roberts–Donaldson ANF) and cross-checked against the known ANF wording; verify verbatim in the citations pass.
text: For it was for this end that the Word of God was made man, and He who was the Son of God became the Son of man, that man, having been taken into the Word, and receiving the adoption, might become the son of God.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: The Eucharist and the resurrection of the flesh — as the bread of earth, receiving God's invocation, is 'no longer common bread' but 'consisting of two realities, earthly and heavenly,' so our bodies, receiving the Eucharist, are 'no longer corruptible, having the hope of the resurrection.' Load-bearing point for the goodness of the material creation and the bodily resurrection, against Gnostic contempt for the flesh. Use for the resurrection-of-the-body case; do NOT deploy to adjudicate intra-Christian eucharistic-mode debates (neutrality guardrail). Captured via web fetch (New Advent, Roberts–Donaldson ANF) and cross-checked against the known ANF wording; verify verbatim in the citations pass.
text: For as the bread, which is produced from the earth, when it receives the invocation of God, is no longer common bread, but the Eucharist, consisting of two realities, earthly and heavenly; so also our bodies, when they receive the Eucharist, are no longer corruptible, having the hope of the resurrection to eternity.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: The classic 'admirable exchange' formula of recapitulation — the Word of God 'did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.' Presupposes Christ's full deity (only God can raise us to His own life) and full humanity (He truly became what we are). Frame the second clause as participation/likeness by grace, not becoming God by nature. Captured via web fetch (New Advent, Roberts–Donaldson ANF) and cross-checked against the known ANF wording; verify verbatim in the citations pass.
text: the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: c. AD 180 — Scripture names no one 'God, definitely and absolutely,' who is not truly God; and so it names the Son. A clean, well-attested pre-Nicene deity-of-Christ witness that strengthens the crown-jewel stat. Quote ends before the Psalm 110:1 proof-text that follows. text: Therefore neither would the Lord, nor the Holy Spirit, nor the apostles, have ever named as God, definitely and absolutely, him who was not God, unless he were truly God; nor would they have named any one in his own person Lord, except God the Father ruling over all, and His Son who has received dominion from His Father over all creation.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: c. AD 180 — the major pre-Nicene defense of the resurrection of the flesh, tied to Christ's own risen body: the nail-marks and the wounded side are the tokens that it was flesh that rose, so it is flesh that will be raised. Adds depth to the Resurrection bucket. Quoted from the numbered section 1 (not the ANF editorial chapter-summary); ends before the inline 1 Corinthians 6:14 reference. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: In the same manner, therefore, as Christ did rise in the substance of flesh, and pointed out to His disciples the mark of the nails and the opening in His side (now these are the tokens of that flesh which rose from the dead), so shall He also, it is said, raise us up by His own power.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: c. AD 180 — a foundational patristic statement of Scripture's inspiration and authority (a core site guardrail): the Scriptures are perfect because they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit. 'Things of that nature' in context are the mysteries Scripture does not fully explain — Irenaeus counsels leaving those to God rather than inventing another god, while holding Scripture perfect. Fills the thin Scripture/authority cluster. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: We should leave things of that nature to God who created us, being most properly assured that the Scriptures are indeed perfect, since they were spoken by the Word of God and His Spirit.

author: Irenaeus of Lyons
note: c. AD 180 — Irenaeus' 'two hands of God' theology: the Son (the Word) and the Spirit (Wisdom) are eternally present with the Father and are those by whom He made all things — a pre-Nicene witness to the co-eternity of the three. Quote ends before the inline Genesis 1:26 citation. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things.
